text: Last lesson left you with a promise: a precise, numeric test separating genuine entanglement from any classical shared-randomness scheme. This lesson delivers it — the same test that won a Nobel Prize and now underpins real cryptographic protocols.

In 1935, Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen argued quantum mechanics must be incomplete. Their reasoning: if measuring one entangled particle lets you predict the other with certainty, that quantity must correspond to some real, pre-existing property — an element of reality. But quantum mechanics says no such definite value exists before measurement. Their conclusion: quantum mechanics must be missing a hidden variable. For decades this was treated as unsettleable philosophy — until 1964, when John Bell found a way to turn the dispute into a number.

Bell's insight, refined into the CHSH inequality: measure each particle of an entangled pair using one of two possible angles per side, call them a, a-prime on one side and b, b-prime on the other. Combine the resulting correlators into S equals E of a-b, minus E of a-b-prime, plus E of a-prime-b, plus E of a-prime-b-prime. Bell's theorem says any local hidden-variable theory, no matter how the script is built, must satisfy the magnitude of S less than or equal to 2. That's a hard mathematical consequence of locality plus predetermined outcomes.

Quantum mechanics predicts the correlator equals negative cosine of the angle difference. Using the standard angles — 0, 90, 45, and 135 degrees — direct computation gives four correlators of magnitude 0.7071 each, three negative and one positive. Combining them into S gives negative 2.8284, so the magnitude of S is 2 root 2, about 2.828 — comfortably exceeding the classical bound of 2. No local hidden-variable theory can produce anything above 2.

This isn't a thought experiment. From Clauser's 1970s experiments through Aspect's 1980s tests to Zeilinger's loophole-closing refinements, real measurements on real entangled particles repeatedly confirm the quantum prediction, not the classical bound — work that shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. And it's now a usable resource: because no classical or faked system can produce a CHSH value above 2, device-independent quantum key distribution uses the measured size of S itself as proof that two parties truly share entanglement, with any eavesdropper's tampering dropping that value back toward 2.
